analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy lower-priced prescription drugs from Canada and other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support from 37 House members, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the current ban on importing prescription drugs and allowed FDA-approved medications to be brought in from Canada, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, and European Union countries through a registered, inspected system. It banned drug manufacturers from discriminating against importers or from making deliberate differences between the U.S. and foreign versions of the same drug, and it let state attorneys general and the Federal Trade Commission enforce those rules. Its stated aim was to close the gap that lets Americans pay several times what consumers abroad pay for the same pills.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially people paying cash or without generous insurance, would gain access to the same FDA-approved drugs sold at lower prices in Canada and Europe. Pharmacies and wholesalers that registered as importers, and foreign pharmacies registered as exporters, would gain a new legal market.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cites congressional findings that Americans pay up to 5 times more than consumers in other countries for the same brand-name drugs, and that drugs cost 35 to 55 percent less in other developed countries [S3].

It would let individuals import up to a 90-day personal supply from registered exporters in Canada and other permitted countries, with a valid U.S. prescription and anti-counterfeiting marking requirements [S3].

It prohibits manufacturers from charging exporters higher prices than local buyers, cutting off or delaying supply to registered exporters, or creating differences between the U.S. version of a drug and the version sold abroad; violations are enforceable by the FTC and state attorneys general [S3].
Reselling in the U.S. a drug properly sold abroad would not count as patent infringement, removing a legal tool used against importers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost: their ability to charge U.S. patients far more than foreign buyers for the same drugs would be curtailed, and they would face new reporting, inspection, and anti-discrimination obligations. The FDA would take on a large new registration and inspection program, funded by fees on importers and exporters that could be passed into drug prices.

drawbacks.text: Importation raises genuine safety questions about supply chains outside FDA's direct control; the bill addresses this with registration, facility inspections at least 12 times a year, chain-of-custody verification, bonds, and recall reporting, but skeptics argued no safeguards fully eliminate counterfeit or diverted-drug risk [S3].

The bill excludes biologics, injected and infused drugs, and controlled substances, so many of the most expensive modern therapies (monoclonal antibodies, for example) would remain off-limits to importation, limiting the savings [S3].

The compliance regime — registration fees, inspection fees capped at 2.5 percent of imported drug value, exporter bonds, and shipping verification — adds real costs that importers would pass to consumers, and manufacturers retained an affirmative defense if a supply cutoff or price difference was not based on importation, creating room for disputes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers paying the world's highest brand-drug prices, the potential savings outweighed the compliance costs, and the bill was unusually detailed about safety rather than a free-for-all. The honest objection is that drug-importation schemes depend on manufacturers' foreign supplies continuing to flow; the bill tried to force this by making supply cutoffs and price discrimination illegal, but whether that enforcement would hold up in practice was the central open question.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry (D-AR) introduced the bill on March 4, 2009, joined by Rep. Jo Ann Emerson (R-MO) as an original co-sponsor, making it bipartisan from day one [S3, S5].
It attracted 37 cosponsors — 22 of 253 House Democrats and 15 of 178 House Republicans [S4].

The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on March 4, 2009, and to that committee's Health Subcommittee the next day; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: U.S. prices stayed free of competition from Canadian and European supplies, and American consumers continued paying more for the same FDA-approved drugs. Congressional importation proposals have died the same way in committee across multiple Congresses, with the industry's Washington presence among the best-funded in lobbying.

for.name: Rep. Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original Republican co-sponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee — Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the entire Congress.

against.name: Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never brought the bill before the committee or subcommittee for action during the 111th Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and brand-name drug manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose U.S. pricing the bill would curtail
against.what_they_did: Opposed prescription drug importation proposals in this era and lobbied against them; the industry's opposition to importation was longstanding and heavily resourced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 37 cosponsors split 22 Democrats and 15 Republicans, and its two named sponsors were a Democrat from Arkansas and a Republican from Missouri; it was never voted on, so no roll call exists to measure a partisan split [S3, S4].

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to end the practice of charging U.S. patients far more than foreign buyers for the same FDA-approved drug: it bans price discrimination against exporters, deliberate U.S./foreign product differences, and supply cutoffs aimed at importers, and it removes patent infringement as a barrier to resale of drugs properly sold abroad [S2, S3]. Every dollar of consumer savings under the bill comes largely out of the industry's U.S. revenue.

industries.industry: Canadian and foreign mail-order pharmacies (would-be registered exporters)
industries.note: Registered exporters meeting licensing, inspection, bond, and privacy requirements would gain a legal channel to sell to American patients; their revenue depends on selling real drugs cheaper, so their interest runs with consumers' [S3].

industries.industry: U.S. pharmacies and drug wholesalers (would-be registered importers)
industries.note: Pharmacies, pharmacy groups, and wholesalers that registered could import qualifying drugs at lower cost, though they would pay a $10,000 registration fee, semiannual inspection fees, and bear marking and recall obligations [S3].

industries.industry: Payment processors and Internet pharmacy platforms
industries.note: The bill bars payment systems from handling transactions with unregistered foreign pharmacies, while registered online sellers would operate legally — tightening the market against rogue sellers while opening it to compliant ones [S2].
